title: ChatGPT No Thing But a Chicken Wing
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Writing just weeks after ChatGPT's public release triggered panic across education circles, Stuart offers a deliberately lukewarm response grounded in his long-running Everest-statement philosophy rather than in expertise on cutting-edge instructional technology. He argues the hype cycle is familiar, echoing past panics around online courses, individualized learning platforms, and remote learning, and that a plain, timeless classroom purpose statement remains relevant regardless of which new tool arrives. He acknowledges ChatGPT could be used cleverly in brainstorming, drafting, or discussion, but says he has no near-term plans to use it himself, expecting the spiral notebook to remain his students' dominant technology. His central argument is that credible teachers need to keep casting a compelling vision of what school is for, since most students don't actually know why they're doing the work, and that vision, not detection or prohibition, is what will make students see cheating with ChatGPT as pointless for their own growth. He closes by reframing the conversation away from adversarial AI-versus-teachers framing toward ongoing, curious conversation with students about the technology.
points: Explicitly declines the expert-on-cutting-edge-instruction framing, positioning his response instead around a stable, pre-existing classroom philosophy (the Everest statement) rather than reactive AI-specific tactics.
Argues most student vulnerability to tools like ChatGPT stems from a deeper problem, students not knowing what school is for, rather than from the technology itself.
Predicts the spiral notebook will remain his students' primary classroom technology even in a ChatGPT world, a concrete claim about how little his practice will change.
Reframes the debate away from an adversarial AI-versus-teachers contest toward ongoing curious conversation with students about the technology's role and limits.
quotes: But first, I'm not an expert on cutting edge instruction. Such expertise holds no interest for me. I do not desire being the best or brightest or most successful.

And so, in a world with ChatGPT cranking out cogent written responses to school prompts, guess what? That old Everest statement is as relevant as it's ever been, thanks completely to the fact that I made it to be plain and timeless.

In the travels and conversations and research and writing that led to my coming book on student motivation, I've become rock-solid convinced of this truth: most students don't know what school is for.

And so, will it be possible for a student to pass off ChatGPT writing for her own in school? I'm sure it will. But will such passing off do much for the growing of the student — for advancing her ability to flourish long-term? I don't think so.
I want to have these conversations curiously, passionately — but not adversarially, not antagonistically, not from a place of "I'm afraid ChatGPT is outmoding my job.
It's not us in contest with our students. It's not us against them. And there's not a technology around that can replace the power of a Credible teacher with students.
